# Aristotelian Motion, Time, and Phantasia: Temporal Awareness in Rhetorical Being

## Articulate Aristotle's Understanding

Aristotle's conception of being emerges from a fundamental engagement with the temporal and kinetic dimensions of existence, where motion and time function not as abstract philosophical categories but as the very conditions through which beings disclose themselves in their essential character. As Heidegger observes in his interpretation of Aristotelian philosophy, the researcher becomes "led by truth itself," where "ἀλήθεια and πρᾶγμα are employed in the same sense, that is, ἀλήθεια is not 'validity,' which adheres to the proposition, or something like that," but rather "πρᾶγμα is nothing other than the being in its being-uncovered, insofar as the being with which I have to do is there in a certain discoveredness" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 176-177). This understanding reveals that Aristotelian being cannot be separated from its temporal manifestation, for beings show themselves precisely through their capacity for change and their embeddedness within durational structures. Burke's analysis reinforces this temporal dimension when (Hawhee 2011) "the selective nature of existence favors some images above others—and high among them, naturally, is the imagery of Life and Death, with its variants of being born, being reborn, dying, killing, and being killed," thus establishing that being's essence emerges through its temporal transformations rather than through static categorical determinations (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 27-28). Indeed, this temporal character of being establishes the foundation for understanding how rhetorical discourse operates not merely as a tool for persuasion but as a fundamental mode through which beings encounter and disclose themselves within their temporal horizons, making rhetoric itself an ontological rather than merely instrumental phenomenon. ## Aristotle on Motion

The Aristotelian concept of motion (kinesis) functions as a fundamental ontological category that reveals the dynamic character of being itself, where motion serves not as accidental change occurring to static substances but as the very mode through which beings actualize their potentialities within temporal frameworks. Heidegger's  "kinesis should be understood as a fundamental way that Dasein is," where motion becomes constitutive of being rather than merely descriptive of particular changes that beings undergo (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 27). The complexity of this understanding emerges through Aristotle's definition of motion as "the fulfillment of the alterable as alterable," which Heidegger renders as "Bewegung ist immer Bewegung eines Bewegten, das durch ein anderes Bewegendes bewegt wird," thereby revealing the intricate relationship between activity and passivity that characterizes all genuine motion (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 27). This  motion cannot be understood through the traditional subject-object dichotomy, for the thing moved participates actively in its own motion while simultaneously being affected by other moving entities. Subsequently, phantasia emerges as particularly significant in this context because it represents a form of psychic motion that enables the soul to apprehend and process temporal transformations; as O'Gorman notes, phantasia operates as "a distinct part of the psyche, essential to all animal action and all human thought, including deliberation, contemplation, and creativity" (O'Gorman, *Aristotle's Phantasia in the Rhetoric*, p. 4). Hence, motion reveals itself as the fundamental condition through which beings engage with their temporal environment, making possible both practical deliberation and theoretical contemplation through the dynamic interplay of potentiality and actuality that characterizes all genuine becoming. ## Aristotle on Time

Aristotelian temporality operates as the measure and condition of motion, where time emerges not as an empty container within which events occur but as the very structure through which beings manifest their essential character through processes of actualization and change. Heidegger's interpretation reveals how Greek thinking conceives time in terms of presence, where being becomes "being-present (Anwesenheit) in the Greek understanding," thus establishing temporal presence as the fundamental horizon within which beings disclose themselves (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 176-177). This  time cannot be separated from the beings that exist within temporal duration, for temporal measurement depends upon the regular motions of particular entities rather than constituting an independent metaphysical framework. The significance of this temporal structure becomes apparent when we recognize that rhetorical discourse operates precisely through temporal synthesis, where past experiences, present circumstances, and future possibilities become integrated through persuasive appeals that address audiences embedded within specific temporal horizons. Thus, Aristotelian time functions not as mere chronological sequence but as the ontological condition through which beings achieve coherence and determinacy through their engagement with changing circumstances; this temporal  rhetorical effectiveness depends upon kairos, the appropriate timing that enables discourse to respond adequately to the temporal dynamics of particular situations, making rhetoric itself a fundamentally temporal art that operates through sensitivity to the temporal rhythms of human existence. ## The Relation Between Motion and Time

The intimate relationship between motion and time in Aristotelian philosophy reveals how temporal awareness emerges through the soul's engagement with changing phenomena, where time becomes the measure of motion while motion provides the experiential content through which temporal duration becomes accessible to consciousness. Rickert's  this relationship operates through what he terms "ambient" engagement, where beings exist not as isolated subjects confronting external temporal processes but as embedded entities whose temporal awareness emerges through their participatory engagement with environmental changes (Rickert, *Ambient Rhetoric*, pp. 53-54). This ambient character of temporal experience means that motion and time cannot be understood as separate metaphysical categories but must be grasped as complementary aspects of the dynamic process through which beings actualize their potentialities within durational frameworks. Burke's examination reinforces this understanding by showing how temporal transformation operates through symbolic processes where " man's timeless essence in temporal terms if, instead of calling him 'by nature a criminal,' you say, 'he will end on the gallows,'" thus revealing how identity and essence emerge through temporal narratives rather than through static categorical determinations (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 27-28). Subsequently, Bowin's analysis reveals how "the being-determined of those beings by δύναμις—ἐνέργεια and the possibility of contexts of movement in beings" establishes motion as the fundamental condition through which temporal experience becomes possible, where potentiality and actuality interact dynamically to produce the temporal synthesis characteristic of conscious experience (referenced through Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 262-263). Hence, the relationship between motion and time establishes the ontological foundation for rhetorical discourse, which operates precisely through the temporal integration of changing circumstances with persuasive responses that enable audiences to navigate their temporal existence through enhanced understanding of their situation and possibilities. ## Aisthēsis and Temporal Awareness

Sensory perception (aisthēsis) operates as the foundational capacity through which beings achieve temporal awareness, establishing the experiential basis for all subsequent temporal synthesis by providing the immediate contact with changing phenomena that enables consciousness to apprehend durational processes. The significance of aisthēsis emerges through its role in making possible the temporal integration that characterizes all conscious experience, where successive sensory impressions become unified through the soul's capacity to retain past impressions while remaining open to present and future experiences. Burke's analysis reveals how this temporal synthesis operates through what he terms the "temporizing of essence," where beings achieve identity and coherence through narrative processes that integrate temporal experience into meaningful patterns (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 27-28). This  temporal awareness cannot be reduced to mere chronological sequence but involves the complex integration of retention, present awareness, and anticipation that enables beings to inhabit their temporal environment coherently. Multiple Authors emphasize how "passions are dispositions oriented on others' dispositions that define our in-the-worldness," where aisthēsis provides the experiential foundation for the emotional and cognitive responses through which beings navigate their temporal circumstances (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115). Indeed, this temporal character of sensory  rhetorical discourse operates primarily through appeals to shared temporal experience rather than through abstract logical demonstration, for audiences respond to persuasive appeals precisely insofar as those appeals resonate with their embodied temporal awareness. Accordingly, aisthēsis establishes the experiential foundation for the temporal awareness that makes possible both practical deliberation and rhetorical effectiveness, demonstrating how sensory engagement with changing circumstances provides the basis for the temporal synthesis through which beings achieve coherent orientation within their dynamic environment. ## Phantasia and Temporal Unification

Phantasia emerges as the crucial faculty through which temporal experience achieves unity and coherence, operating as the psychic capacity that enables consciousness to synthesize successive temporal moments into integrated experiential wholes that can serve as the foundation for deliberation, memory, and anticipation. 4). This temporal unifying function operates through phantasia's capacity to preserve sensory impressions beyond their immediate temporal presence, creating what O'Gorman describes as "after-images of phantasia, this residue of sense perception," which enable consciousness to integrate past experience with present circumstances and future possibilities (O'Gorman, *Aristotle's Phantasia in the Rhetoric*, p. 4). The significance of this temporal integration becomes apparent when we recognize that effective deliberation requires the ability to envision future possibilities based upon past experience while remaining responsive to present circumstances, a complex temporal synthesis that phantasia makes possible through its imaging capacity. Multiple Authors emphasize how this temporal function operates specifically in rhetorical contexts, where "fear becomes present to us not by direct experience, aisthesis, but through our imagination, phantasia; fancies replace sensations as stimulus," thus demonstrating how phantasia enables rhetorical discourse to operate through temporal projection rather than merely through present sensory appeal (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115). Burke's analysis reinforces this understanding by showing how imaginative synthesis enables the "transformation" processes through which beings achieve coherent identity across temporal change, where phantasia provides the psychic capacity for the symbolic processes through which temporal experience becomes meaningful (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 27-28). Hence, phantasia establishes the temporal unification that makes possible both effective deliberation and persuasive discourse, demonstrating how imaginative synthesis enables beings to inhabit their temporal existence coherently through the integration of past, present, and future within unified experiential wholes. ## Heidegger's Interpretation of Aristotle

Heidegger's reading of Aristotelian philosophy reveals how ancient Greek thinking anticipates fundamental insights into the temporal and kinetic character of being, where Aristotelian concepts such as kinesis, phantasia, and the passions (pathē) disclose the essentially temporal structure of human existence in ways that modern philosophy has largely obscured through its emphasis on static conceptual analysis. The crucial insight emerges through Heidegger's recognition that "kinesis gives the authentic Da-Charakter to Dasein, the vital place-time of Being," thus revealing how motion functions not as accidental change but as the fundamental mode through which beings exist temporally (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115). 115). Bowin's analysis supports this temporal interpretation by showing how Aristotelian temporal awareness operates through "the perception and cognition of time" as integrated processes that reveal the essential temporality of conscious existence (Bowin, *Aristotle on the Perception and Cognition of Time*, referenced in knowledge units). The significance of this interpretation extends beyond historical scholarship to reveal how rhetorical discourse operates through what Heidegger identifies as fundamentally temporal structures, where "fear sets us thinking what could be done," or "fear makes us deliberators," thus demonstrating how emotional engagement with temporal possibilities enables the practical deliberation characteristic of political existence (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115). Subsequently, this Heideggerian reading reveals how Aristotelian concepts provide resources for understanding rhetorical effectiveness as fundamentally grounded in temporal awareness, where persuasive discourse succeeds precisely insofar as it enables audiences to achieve coherent orientation within their temporal circumstances through enhanced understanding of their possibilities and limitations within changing historical conditions. ---
